description:
The Super Lead, and 1959 is its part number rather than its year — it arrived in 1965 and defined everything after it.

Two channels with four inputs, meant to be jumpered together with a short cable so you can blend the bright channel against the normal one. That trick is half the sound, and it is the first thing to try here.

It wants to be loud and it rewards you for it. Below halfway it is a stiff clean amp; past that the power section starts to give and the whole thing opens up.

The 50-watt Plexi, and the one that actually turns up on records more than its bigger brother does.

Half the power means it breaks up at a volume a room can survive, and a 50-watt Marshall pushed hard has a looser, warmer low end than a 100 doing the same job. Engineers worked this out early and never went back.

Same four inputs, same jumper trick, same absence of a gain knob. If the 100 feels too tight and too clean for where you have the volume set, this is the one.

The 5150 III, and Eddie Van Halen's last amp design — built with EVH rather than Peavey, and a deliberate correction of the original.

Three channels, EL34s in the 100-watt version, and a tighter, more modern low end with the 5150's harshness sanded off. The blue channel is the one everybody uses.

The 5F6-A tweed Bassman: built for a bass guitar, ignored by bass players, and adopted by everybody else.

Four 10-inch speakers and a tone stack that became the tone stack — Jim Marshall copied this circuit almost exactly to build his first amp, so every British amp in this list is descended from it.

It does not stay clean for long and it was never meant to. Pushed, it is the sound of a Telecaster in a small room, and it still does blues better than anything built since.

basedOn: Dweezil Zappa's 1965 blackface Fender Bassman, AB165
description:
The blackface Bassman, which is a different amp from the tweed despite the name. Fender scooped the midrange and stiffened the power section.

Cleaner, louder and far less willing to break up — a pedal platform before anybody used that phrase. Where the tweed gives you its own character, this one gives you yours.

The Champ. One volume knob, one 8-inch speaker, five watts, and an unreasonable number of famous solos.

It is far too small for a stage and exactly right in front of a microphone, which is why it lived in studios for decades. Turn it up and it distorts immediately — there is nothing else for it to do.

The sound is small, urgent and slightly falling apart, and no big amp turned down will imitate it.

basedOn: Fender Narrow Panel high-powered Tweed Twin, 5F8
description:
The high-powered tweed Twin — the loudest thing Fender made in the fifties and, for a while, the loudest thing anyone made.

Two 12s and four output valves, with enough headroom to stay clean at volumes the smaller tweeds could not approach. Push it past that and you get an enormous, slow, three-dimensional distortion that the blackface amps traded away for cleanliness.

A brown-panel Super from 1960 — the short window between the tweed amps and the blackface ones, when Fender was still figuring out what it wanted.

Two 10s, harmonic tremolo, and a midrange that sits between the warmth of the tweeds and the glass of the blackface. The brown amps are the connoisseur's Fenders for exactly this reason.

The brown Concert: four 10-inch speakers, which is the Bassman cabinet, wearing the brown-era circuit.

More punch and a firmer low end than the two-speaker amps of the same period, and the same slightly woody midrange.

Morgan's AC20 — a modern British-voiced amp with an AC30 heart and twenty watts of it.

Chime and grind at a volume that works in a small room, with better build quality than the amp it descends from.

The Engl Savage: a lot of gain, a lot of control, and a very tight low end.

German high gain is a recognisable thing — more compressed and more focused than British or American amps, with an almost synthetic evenness to the distortion. This is the archetype.

The PRS Archon: a lot of gain from a company better known for guitars, and a genuinely excellent clean channel underneath it.

Smooth rather than aggressive, with a clarity in the high end that suits it to lead playing.

Mark Cameron built his reputation modifying Marshalls to an extreme degree, and the Atomica is one of his own designs rather than a modified amp.

Made in small numbers and rarely seen. If you own one you know more about it than this catalogue does.

A blackface Bandmaster head — the AB763 circuit, which is the one Fender got right and then used in almost everything.

Clean, bright, and generous with headroom, with the scooped midrange that makes a Stratocaster sound like a Stratocaster. It is a platform more than a voice.

The Blankenship Leeds 21 — a hand-built California amp in the British tradition, voiced closer to a Hiwatt than to a Vox.

Clean, firm and made in very small numbers, which is most of why you have not heard one.

The Bludotone Ojai, one of the better-regarded Dumble-style builds.

A Fender-voiced clean with a smooth overdrive on top, and the responsiveness to the guitar volume that the whole style is built around.

The Fish — Bogner's rack preamp from the early nineties, and one of the strangest-looking pieces of gear in this catalogue.

Five voicings covering the Bogner range, all in one rack unit. Steve Vai used one for years.

The JCM800 2203, and the sound of the eighties with the volume up. Marshall added a master volume, which meant for the first time you could get the amp's distortion without the amp's full output.

That one change made thrash possible. It is tighter and more mid-forward than a Plexi, with a hard edge to the top that cuts through anything — and it stays articulate when you play fast, which the older amps do not.

Very little gain by modern standards. If it sounds thin, that is the amp asking for a pedal in front of it, which is exactly how most of those records were made.

basedOn: Marshall Studio Classic SC20, a 20-watt JCM800
description:
The JCM800 shrunk to 20 watts. Same preamp, same master volume, far less air being moved.

It gives up some of the big amp's authority in the low end and gains a little immediacy in return. For recording it is arguably the more useful of the two.

Marshall's attempt to bottle one specific night: Slash's rhythm sound on Appetite for Destruction, which came from a heavily modified amp nobody could buy.

So they built it. More gain and more low end than a stock Plexi, with the midrange pushed forward where a Les Paul lives, and a presence control that will take your head off if you let it.

The other side of the AFD100 — Marshall's signature Slash head, voiced towards the older, cleaner Super Lead behaviour rather than its modified channel.

Use it where you want the Appetite amp's body without its gain.

The first Marshall. Jim Marshall's shop copied a Fender Bassman almost part for part, then changed the valves and the speakers — and got something that sounded nothing like a Fender.

KT66 output valves and a valve rectifier give it a soft, forgiving compression: notes swell rather than snap. Clapton made the Beano record with one and set the template for British blues rock in about forty minutes.

Warmer and rounder than every Marshall that followed. If a Plexi sounds too aggressive, this is where to go.

Marshall's own answer to the question of which Marshall you want: all of them.

Four channels, three voices each, which walks from a JTM 45 through a Plexi and a JCM800 to more gain than Marshall had ever put in a production amp. The models here are the two overdrive channels, which is where most people live.

They have a great deal of gain on tap. Start with Input Drive lower than feels right and come up — this amp will happily give you more than the song wants.

The JMP-1, a rack preamp from 1992, and for a decade the quiet centre of an awful lot of professional rigs.

It is Marshall's voicings under MIDI control with no power section of its own, which made it the first Marshall you could switch silently mid-song. That convenience is why it turns up on so many records from that period.

The Silver Jubilee, built in 1987 for Marshall's twenty-fifth year and then wanted forever afterwards.

It runs its output valves in a half-power pentode mode and uses diode clipping in the preamp, which sounds like it should be a compromise and instead produces a thick, vocal midrange that no other Marshall has. Slash toured on them; Frusciante recorded on one.

More gain than a JCM800 and more body than a JVM. The rhythm/lead clip switch is the whole amp in one button.

Budda's Twinmaster — a small EL84 amp from the nineties, voiced warm and loose rather than chimey.

It was one of the first modern low-wattage boutique amps and a lot of what followed took its cue from it.

The Custom Audio 3+ SE: Bob Bradshaw's rack preamp, and the heart of an enormous number of professional rigs in the late eighties and nineties.

Three channels, MIDI switching, and a clean channel good enough that people used the preamp for that alone. Bradshaw built the rigs; this is what was usually in them.

The amp Mark Cameron's Marshall modifications eventually turned into — a British circuit taken a long way past where Marshall left it.

Built in small numbers and hard to find second hand.

The HOOK Captain 34 — a hand-built European boutique amp made in very small numbers.

There is little written about it anywhere, and this catalogue would rather say that than guess.

The Carr Rambler — a boutique American amp built around the blackface Fender idea, with an attenuator so it can break up at any volume.

Clean, chiming, and unusually well made.

Carol-Ann's OD2, a hand-built American amp aimed at high gain, made in very small numbers by one builder.

Rare enough that most players will never meet one outside a model like this.

The Carol-Ann Triptik: three channels, hand built, and produced in tiny quantities.

Another amp most people will only ever hear as a model rather than in a room.

The Tucana 3 — Carol-Ann's American-voiced amp, built around clean headroom rather than modern high gain.

Hand built in very small numbers, and seldom seen outside the hands of the people who ordered one.

The Orange AD30: EL84s, no master volume, and a midrange that will not be argued with.

British class A in the Vox tradition but darker and thicker, with far more low-mid weight. It is a very forward-sounding amp and it does not disappear in a band.

Orange's AD200B: valve bass amplification with the Orange midrange, which is thick, warm and slightly rude.

Less scooped than an SVT and more obviously coloured. Geezer Butler's sound in a box.

The Rockerverb — Orange's high-gain amp, and the one that made the brand credible to metal players.

Thick, warm saturation with the Orange midrange underneath it, and a clean channel with real reverb. Less scooped than an American high-gain amp and much easier to hear in a mix.

The Tiny Terror: fifteen watts, two knobs and a handle, and the amp that started the entire small-valve-head boom of the 2000s.

Almost no controls and no clean headroom to speak of. Turn it up, play, and it does one very good thing.

The AC15 with Top Boost — half the power and a single 12, which is the AC30 sound at a volume a normal room can take.

It breaks up considerably earlier than the 30, which for most people is an advantage rather than a compromise.

The AC30 without Top Boost — the original, which is brighter and more raw than the version everyone means when they say AC30.

No negative feedback and cathode bias, so it compresses and blooms rather than staying stiff. The Beatles made their early records on these.

Chiming when clean, and when pushed it gets a ragged upper-midrange bark that nothing else quite does.

The AC30 Top Boost: an extra valve stage and a proper treble and bass control, added because players kept asking for more high end.

That circuit is the British jangle — Brian May's entire sound is one of these with a treble booster in front, and The Edge built U2 on the clean channel with delay.

Push the volume and it does not so much distort as fray, brilliantly, in the upper mids.

The Komet 60, built to a Ken Fischer design after his death — the Trainwreck idea in a slightly more practical amp.

Extremely touch-sensitive, very little compression, and expensive.
Komet's Concorde: more gain and more modern voicing than the Komet 60, while keeping the responsiveness that the brand is built on.

The Cornford MK50 II — a British hand-built amp with a tight, modern gain structure over a traditional EL34 power section.

Cornford made relatively few amps and they are well regarded by people who found them.

The Diezel VH4, and the sound of German engineering applied to distortion.

Four independent channels, each with its own everything, and a high-gain voice that is tight, dark and enormous all at once. Adam Jones built Tool's sound on one; Metallica have used them for years.

It is not a warm amp. It is a precise one, and at high gain that precision is the entire appeal.

The brown Deluxe. Twenty watts, one 12, and the brown-panel harmonic tremolo, which is a genuinely different effect from the amplitude tremolo that replaced it.

It breaks up early and gracefully and it is one of the best small amps Fender ever built.

The 5E3 tweed Deluxe, and the most copied small amp in the world.

Cathode-biased with no negative feedback, which in practice means it sags, blooms and compresses under your hands in a way modern amps do not. The two volume controls interact — turning one up changes the other — and learning that interaction is learning the amp.

Neil Young has used one for fifty years. It is small, loose and completely alive.

The blackface Deluxe Reverb: probably the most recorded guitar amp ever built.

Twenty-two watts is loud enough for a club and quiet enough to break up on stage, and the reverb and tremolo are the standard everyone else is measured against. Clean up to about five, then a warm, gentle overdrive after that.

If you do not know which amp to start from, start from this one.

The Diamond Del Fuego, a hand-built amp from a small Canadian maker better known for its pedals.

Produced in limited numbers and not widely documented anywhere.

Friedman's blues amp: a single channel, 40 watts, and none of the BE-100's gain.

Built around an old JTM-ish voice rather than a modern one — it cleans up completely with the guitar volume and it wants a Les Paul.

Divided by 13's CJ 11 — a small, beautifully built American-voiced amp in the tweed tradition.

Low powered and quick to break up, with a midrange richer than the wattage suggests.

The FTR 37, Divided by 13's best-known amp: 37 watts, with real reverb and tremolo and a clean sound somewhere between a Fender and a Vox.

It stays clean far longer than the small Div/13 amps and it takes pedals well.

The VH4 again — four channels, each fully independent, and a high-gain character that is tight and dark rather than bright and raw.

The amp for people who found Rectifiers too loose and Marshalls too thin.

The Twin Reverb. Eighty-five watts into two 12s, and effectively impossible to make distort at any volume a human can be in a room with.

That is the point of it. It is the reference clean amp — country, jazz, funk, anything with a pedalboard in front of it — and the loudest clean sound in this catalogue.

basedOn: Dweezil Zappa's modded 1965 blackface Fender Bassman, AB165
description:
Dweezil Zappa's blackface Bassman, modified away from clean and towards gain.

The blackface chassis with more preamp in front of it: the tight, scooped bottom end of the original with something to push against.

The Engl Powerball, built for speed. Extremely tight, extremely fast, with a treble response that cuts through anything.

A generation of European metal bands recorded on these.

The Bogner Ecstasy: Reinhold Bogner's take on what a hot-rodded Marshall should have been, and one of the most flattering amps ever built.

Three channels, and a set of small switches — structure, excursion, plexi mode — that change the amp's character far more than they sound like they should. The midrange is rich and slightly compressed and it makes almost everything sound expensive.

Less aggressive than a Friedman, more complex than a JCM800.

The Uberschall — Bogner's high-gain amp, and a genuinely nasty one.

Huge saturated low end with a tight attack on top of it, built for downtuned playing. Where the Ecstasy flatters, this one flattens.

Fuchs's Overdrive Supreme — one of the amps built to make the Dumble sound available to people without a Dumble.

The same idea: a clean Fender-derived voice with a smooth, vocal overdrive stacked on top, and unusual sensitivity to picking.

The BE-100. Dave Friedman spent twenty years modifying Marshalls for touring professionals and then built the amp those modifications were reaching for.

It is a Plexi with the gain, low end and tightness that a Plexi never had, and it keeps the original's feel underneath. Jerry Cantrell's rig is built on one.

BE stands for Brown Eye. It is the most Marshall-sounding amp that is not a Marshall.

basedOn: Friedman BE-100, HBE (hot British eq) channel
description:
The BE-100's other channel — HBE, for Hot British Eq, which is the same amp with considerably more gain and a bigger bottom end.

Where BE is a hot Plexi, this is a hot JCM800 with the restraint removed.

Friedman's smaller head, voiced closer to a 50-watt Plexi than to the BE-100.

Less gain, more immediacy, and a looser feel. The one to reach for when the BE is too much amp.

Steven Fryette's Deliverance: high gain without the scooped midrange that most high-gain amps rely on.

The result is an amp that sits in a mix instead of disappearing under the bass. Drier and more honest than a Rectifier.

A mid-sixties Gibson Scout. Gibson made amplifiers for decades and almost nobody remembers them, which is why the good ones are still affordable.

Dark, loose and woody, with a soft break-up. A different flavour of American small amp from the Fenders everyone reaches for.

The Diezel Herbert: more power than the VH4 and a mid-cut control that lets you scoop or push the midrange without touching the EQ.

Brutal, articulate, and one of the few amps that stays clear with everything turned up.

The Hiwatt DR103: built in London by Dave Reeves to military wiring standards, and the cleanest 100-watt valve amp ever made.

Where a Marshall breaks up, a Hiwatt just gets louder. Pete Townshend used them because nothing else survived him; Gilmour used them because the headroom let every pedal in front be heard exactly as it was.

If you want an amp that adds nothing and takes nothing away, this is it.

The Bad Cat Hot Cat: class A EL84 power with far more gain than that arrangement usually has.

British top end over an American amount of distortion, which is an unusual combination and the reason people buy them.

The JMP-1 again — Marshall's MIDI rack preamp, which put four switchable Marshall voices in one rack space and changed how touring rigs were built.

No power valves of its own, so it leans harder on whatever comes after it than a head does.

The Blues Junior: fifteen watts, one 12, EL84s, and the most common small valve amp of the last thirty years.

EL84s give it a brighter, more aggressive break-up than the 6V6 Fenders. It is not subtle and it was never expensive, and it has been on more bar stages than anything else here.

basedOn: Marshall JVM410HJS, Joe Satriani's signature amp
description:
Joe Satriani's JVM, rebuilt around how he actually uses an amp: fewer voices, cleaner switching, and a lead channel with the low end tightened so fast legato stays readable.

Smoother and less grainy than the standard JVM. Built for sustained single notes rather than chugging.

The Roland JC-120: solid state, 120 watts, and the only transistor amp in this list that anybody wants on purpose.

It has no valve warmth at all, which is the point — it is relentlessly clean and it has the best stereo chorus ever built into an amplifier. Andy Summers, Robert Smith and a whole generation of post-punk built their sound on that chorus.

Metallica have used them for clean tones for decades.

basedOn: Carvin Legacy VL100, Steve Vai's signature amp
description:
Carvin's Legacy — Steve Vai's signature amp, and the one his live sound ran on for years.

Voiced for sustain and smoothness rather than attack, with a midrange that keeps single notes singing.

The Matchless Chieftain: EL34s rather than the EL84s Matchless are known for, which gives it more headroom and a more American low end.

The Matchless build quality applied to a cleaner, bigger-sounding amp.

The Matchless DC-30: a Vox AC30 rebuilt by people who cared about every component in it, with two quite different channels.

One channel is chime and the other is a darker, fatter sound closer to a tweed Fender. Point-to-point wired, absurdly expensive, and genuinely one of the best amps ever built.

The Dr. Z Route 66 — the bigger, American-voiced amp in the line, with 6L6s and considerably more headroom.

Cleaner and firmer than the Maz amps, and a fine pedal platform.

The Maz 8: eight watts, and a genuinely usable recording amp that breaks up almost immediately.

Small, warm and very easy to work with in front of a microphone.

Dr. Z's Maz 38 — EL34s, a cut control rather than a conventional treble, and a big, thick clean sound.

Dr. Z amps are built around the idea that fewer controls, chosen well, beat a full tone stack. Brad Paisley has used them for years.

The Swart Atomic Space Tone: a small, dark, tweed-descended amp with real spring reverb and a tube tremolo that is the reason most people buy one.

It is not a loud amp or a clean one. It is atmosphere in a box.

A Dumble Overdrive Special, which is the most mythologised amplifier in existence: Howard Dumble built them one at a time, for people he approved of, and potted the circuit so nobody could copy it.

What it actually does is turn a clean Fender voice into a singing overdrive that keeps every bit of the guitar's character underneath. Robben Ford and Larry Carlton built entire careers on that sound.

It is extremely responsive to the guitar's volume control. Roll back and it cleans up completely.

The block-letter 5150 — Peavey building Eddie Van Halen an amp in 1992, and accidentally building the amp that metalcore would run on for the next thirty years.

It is not subtle and it is not refined. It has a hard upper midrange, an enormous amount of gain, and an attack that cuts through a mix with no help at all.

Cheap, everywhere, and completely unkillable.

The 6505+, which added a second channel with its own controls and became the standard amp of an entire scene.

Marginally tighter and better behaved than the block-letter. If a record between 2000 and 2015 has a rhythm guitar sound you like, there is a fair chance this is it.

The amp the electric guitar sounds like. Four inputs, no master volume, and one decision to make: how loud you are willing to be.

Turned down it is a clean amp with a bit of hair. Turned up it does the thing nothing else does — the note blooms, sits still for a second, then starts to sing. That is the whole sixties and most of the seventies in one circuit.

There is no gain control because there is no gain stage to control. Volume IS the gain, which is why the records were made in rooms nobody could stand to be in.

basedOn: Marshall Studio Vintage SV20, a 20-watt Plexi
description:
A Plexi that fits in a cupboard. Marshall built the Studio Vintage as a real 20-watt valve amp rather than a smaller-sounding imitation of a big one.

The point is that it saturates at a volume you can use. Everything the big Plexi does at deafening it does at loud, which on a modelled version matters less — but the voicing is genuinely a little tighter and drier, and that is worth having as a choice.

The Princeton without the reverb: twelve watts, a 10-inch speaker, and almost no controls.

A practice amp that turned into a studio amp because it does one thing extremely well — it distorts politely at a volume that does not need a separate room.

The blackface Princeton Reverb, which is the small Fender everybody eventually wants.

It has the Deluxe's reverb and tremolo in a cabinet half the size, and it starts breaking up around four — early enough to be useful on a session and late enough to stay clean when you roll the guitar back.

The two-channel Dual Rectifier — the amp the nineties sounded like once grunge turned into everything after it.

Enormous, loose low end and a scooped, saturated midrange, with a valve rectifier you can switch in to make the whole thing sag and bloom under a hard pick attack. It is not a tight amp and that is the point of it.

It needs a cabinet that can move air and it does not reward timid playing.

The three-channel Rectifier, which added a proper clean channel and tidied up the gain structure.

Each channel has its own voicing switch — Raw, Vintage and Modern — and Modern is where the metal is: more gain, tighter bottom, more aggression. Vintage is the older Recto sound.

Smoother and more controllable than the two-channel, which is a trade some people never accepted.

The Revv Generator: a modern Canadian high-gain amp built for tight, aggressive, downtuned playing.

Four aggression levels per channel and a low end that stays defined no matter how far down you tune. One of the tightest amps here.

Paul Ruby's Rocket, built by hand in quantities small enough that most owners know each other.

Almost nothing is documented about it, so nothing about its character is claimed here.

The Ampeg SVT. Three hundred valve watts into eight 10-inch speakers, weighing more than the person carrying it, and the standard by which rock bass is measured.

It has an enormous midrange and it grinds rather than distorts when pushed. Every record you think has a big bass sound probably has one of these on it.

The Shiva: Bogner's middle ground, with more clean headroom than an Ecstasy and a drive channel that stops short of the Uberschall.

The most usable Bogner for someone playing more than one style in a night.

The X88R: the SLO preamp in a rack, from the years when everybody's rig was a rack.

Soldano's overdrive voice with no power section of its own.
The X99, Soldano's programmable rack preamp — the SLO sound under MIDI control.

The SLO-100: Mike Soldano took a Marshall, added preamp stages and built it to a standard nobody was building amps to in 1987.

The result is the template for every modern high-gain amp that followed — enormous smooth sustain with the note still intact underneath it, and a clean channel that is genuinely good rather than an afterthought.

Clapton used one, Gary Moore used one, and Bogner and Friedman both grew out of what it proved was possible.

Splawn's Nitro — a modified Marshall taken further, with switchable gear settings that stack more preamp in front of you.

British bones, modern gain, and a very aggressive upper midrange.

The Splawn Quick Rod: three gears of gain over a Marshall-derived circuit, with a tighter and more scooped voice than the Nitro.

Built for people who wanted a JCM800 that could keep up with a Rectifier.

The Badger 18: a small British-voiced amp with a built-in power scaling control, so you can get full power-section saturation at almost any volume.

That control is the whole idea of the amp and it works.

The Badger 30 — the bigger Badger, with EL34s and more headroom before it gives way.

Same power scaling, and enough headroom to stay clean with a band behind you.

The blackface Super Reverb: four 10-inch speakers, forty-five watts, and the loudest small-speaker sound Fender made.

Four 10s move air differently from a pair of 12s — tighter, faster, with more bite in the upper mids. It is the blues amp for people who found the Twin too polite and the Deluxe too small.

A Supro Dual-Tone. Supro amps were cheap in the sixties and are not now — Jimmy Page recorded the first Led Zeppelin record on one.

Small, raw and mid-heavy, with a tremolo that is part of the sound rather than an effect on top of it. It distorts almost immediately and it sounds enormous on tape.

Supro's modern reissue-in-spirit: the vintage Supro voice, built properly, with a little more control.

Thick, woolly, mid-forward, and completely unlike a Fender of the same size.

The Lone Star, which is Boogie building a Fender rather than a Boogie.

A genuinely beautiful clean channel with real headroom, and a drive channel that stays warm and open instead of going for gain. Made for people who want a Twin that can also get dirty.

A pre-Rev-G Dual Rectifier, which is the early production revision collectors chase and Meshuggah built a career on.

The earliest Rectos had less low-end cut and a more aggressive upper midrange than the ones that followed. Played clean it is unremarkable; played through a downtuned guitar with the gain up it is unmistakable.

The Tremolux — a Deluxe with more power and a separate cabinet, sitting between the Deluxe Reverb and the Bassman.

6L6s rather than 6V6s, so it stays cleaner longer, and the tremolo is the reason to own one.

Boogie's Triple Crown, which is the company deliberately building a British-sounding amp — EL34 output valves rather than their usual 6L6s.

Tighter and more mid-forward than a Rectifier, and much closer to a hot-rodded Marshall than anything else in the Boogie line.

Two-Rock's Jet 35 — another amp in the Dumble tradition, built for clean headroom and a thick, singing lead sound.

Beautifully made, very clean, and expensive.

A wall of 6L6s. Boogie's Bass 400 uses twelve output valves, which is an absurd way to build a bass amp and produces a warmth solid-state rigs cannot get near.

Heavy in both senses. Still used by people who will carry it.

basedOn: Mesa/Boogie JP-2C, the John Petrucci Mark IIC+
description:
Boogie's reissue of the IIC+ built to John Petrucci's specification, which is to say: the famous amp, available again, with a second lead channel and proper MIDI switching.

The IIC+ voice with none of the maintenance and none of the price.

The most expensive used amp in this list, and the reason is one record: Master of Puppets.

Boogie built the Mark series around a cascading preamp and a five-band graphic EQ, and the IIC+ is the revision where all of it came together. The famous setting is a V shape on the EQ sliders, which scoops the mids out and leaves an attack like a hammer.

It is tight where a Rectifier is loose, and it stays readable under fast picking in a way almost nothing else does.

A IIC+ that has been modified further — more gain, more low end, and less of the original's restraint.

If the standard IIC+ feels like it is holding something back, this is the version that does not.

The Mark IV: three channels, the graphic EQ, and more usable range than any Boogie before it.

Smoother and more polished than the IIC+, with a lead channel that sings rather than barks. John Petrucci and Mark Tremonti both spent years on one.

The graphic EQ is not a fine adjustment, it is the main tone control. Move the sliders a long way.

The Mark V, which contains most of the Mark series inside it — three channels with three modes each, covering everything from the tweed-voiced clean up to the IIC+ and IV lead sounds.

The most versatile amp Boogie has built, and the most complicated.

The Subway Blues — a tiny Boogie with EL84s, made for club stages and people who had decided Boogies were too clinical.

Loose, bright and quick to break up. Nothing like the Mark series.

The TriAxis — Boogie's Mark series compressed into a rack preamp, and the cornerstone of an awful lot of early-nineties rigs.

Five voicings, MIDI control and the graphic EQ, with no output valves of its own. Petrucci, Vai and Lukather all built rigs around it.

The Vibro-King: Fender's Custom Shop building a tweed-and-blackface hybrid that never actually existed in the sixties.

Three 10-inch speakers, real spring reverb, and the best tremolo Fender has ever put in a production amp. Expensive, heavy, and worth it.

A brown-panel Vibrolux — the 6G11 circuit, with the harmonic tremolo the brown amps are collected for.

Thirty watts and a single 12. Warmer and woodier than the blackface Vibrolux Reverb that replaced it.

The Vibroverb, the first Fender amp with reverb built into it, and made for barely a year.

Stevie Ray Vaughan built his sound on a pair of them. Forty watts, and a bottom end considerably bigger than the size of the amp suggests.

A Trainwreck. Ken Fischer built about a hundred amps by hand before he died and they now cost more than a car.

The Express is the aggressive one — enormously touch-sensitive, with almost no compression, so everything you do with your hands comes straight out. It is unforgiving and it is the reason people talk about these in the way they do.

No master volume, no effects loop, nothing but the circuit.

The Liverpool is Fischer's British-voiced Trainwreck — EL84s, and a chimier, more open sound than the Express.

Same brutal honesty about your playing, in a Vox accent rather than a Marshall one.

The Rocket: the smallest Trainwreck, with 6V6s and an American flavour.

Warmer and rounder than the other two, and the most forgiving of the three — which for a Trainwreck is not saying a great deal.
